cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: The five main aims of sentencing are: retribution (punishing the offender for what they have done), deterrence (discouraging the offender or others from reoffending), rehabilitation (reforming the offender to prevent future crime), incapacitation (protecting the public by removing dangerous offenders) and reparation (making the offender compensate the victim or society)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Deterrence is divided into individual deterrence (discouraging the specific offender) and general deterrence (discouraging others from committing similar offences)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: The Sentencing Council issues guidelines that courts must follow unless it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so, ensuring consistency in sentencing

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Custodial sentences include: detention for offenders under 18, imprisonment for adult offenders, and life sentences for the most serious offences including murder (which carries a mandatory life sentence)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Community orders under the Sentencing Act 2020 can include requirements such as unpaid work, curfew, drug rehabilitation, attendance at specified activities and prohibitions on travel

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Fines are the most common sentence in the Magistrates' Court; they must be based on the offender's ability to pay and the seriousness of the offence

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Discharges are used for minor offences: absolute discharge (no penalty at all) or conditional discharge (no penalty unless the offender commits a further offence within a set period)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Aggravating factors increase the seriousness of an offence and may lead to a harsher sentence — e.g. use of a weapon, vulnerability of the victim, previous convictions, racially or religiously motivated offending

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Mitigating factors reduce the seriousness and may lead to a more lenient sentence — e.g. pleading guilty, lack of previous convictions, the offender's age, mental health issues, acting under duress

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: A guilty plea typically attracts a reduction in sentence of up to one-third if made at the earliest opportunity, under the Sentencing Council's reduction for guilty plea guideline

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: Sentencing for young offenders (under 18) prioritises rehabilitation and uses different sentences including referral orders, youth rehabilitation orders and detention at a young offender institution

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sentencing & Punishment
cards.back: The principle of proportionality requires that the sentence must be proportionate to the seriousness of the offence and the culpability of the offender

cards.front: What should you know about gcse law exam tips — sentencing & punishment?
cards.back: 1. For Sentencing & Punishment questions, identify the relevant area of law and state the legal principles clearly 2. Apply legal rules to the facts of the scenario — don't just state the law 3. When evaluating, consider both the effectiveness and fairness of legal rules 4. Reference relevant cases and statutes when discussing Sentencing & Punishment 5. Consider reform proposals and alternative approaches where relevant
